items.title: Hy-4 Preview (Fully FREE): RIP Astra? This model is PRETTY CRAZY!
items.summary:
Checkout Hy-4 Preview on WorkBuddy here: https://www.workbuddy.ai/
Thank you to Tencent for sponsoring this video.

In this video, I’ll tell you about Tencent’s new open-weight Hy4 Preview model, a 770-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model built for coding agents, long-horizon planning, tool use, and office productivity. I’ll also show you how to use Hy4 Preview for free with WorkBuddy and test it with complex coding, 3D game development, expense auditing, and research presentation tasks.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 Hy4 Preview is a 770-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 49 billion active parameters.
🧠 Its Gated Sparse Attention mechanism supports a context window of more than 1 million tokens.
🤖 The model is designed for agentic coding, multi-step planning, tool calling, and long-horizon task execution.
📊 Hy4 Preview delivers highly competitive results across GPQA Diamond, Terminal Bench, and SWE-bench Multilingual.
💸 Its affordable API pricing makes it one of the cheapest
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: [music] Hi, welcome to another video. So, Tencent has just released an open-sourced Hi-4 preview, which is their next generation model. And this one is a pretty big deal. It's a 770 billion parameter mixture of experts model with 49 billion active parameters, and it has a context window of over 1 million tokens. It's released under Apache 2.0, zero and the weights are up on hugging face in both BF-16 and FP8 builds. Now, the part that I find really interesting is that this model is not just another chat model. It's been built specifically for agentic work. So, things like coding agents, multi-step planning, long horizon task execution, tool calling, and office productivity stuff like decks and spreadsheets. And the other interesting bit is that Tencent says Hi4 preview actually helped optimize its own training pipeline including the kernels and that increased endto-end throughput by around 31.8% against their baseline which is kind of wild if you think about it. In this video I'll talk about what the model is, what it can actually do, how you can use it for free right now with WorkBuddy, and then I'll show you some demos where I throw some pretty hard tasks at it. So let's get right into it. First, let's talk about the model itself. Like I said, it's 770 billion total parameters, but only 49 billion are active per token. They're using 256 routed experts plus one shared expert with eight experts activated at a time. And they've also got this gated sparse attention mechanism, which is what lets them push the context window past a million tokens without the inference cost going through the roof. On the benchmarks, it's sitting right at the top of the openweight pack. It gets 92.3 on GPQA diamond, 85.4 4 on terminal bench and 82.9 on SWEBench multilingual. It also leads the openw weightight field on a couple of the newer research benchmarks like horizon math and biio mystery bench. Tencent also did an internal blind evaluation with 163 experts across 203 real engineering tasks and high for preview scored 2.99 out of four compared to 2.94 for Kim K3 and 2.92 for GLM 5.3. Now I'm saying internal because it is their only eval. So take it with a grain of salt, but from what I can see, it's basically trading wins with Kimmy K3 and GLM 5.3 across the public benchmarks, and it's still a bit behind the closed models like Opus 5 and GPT 5.6 on most things, which is expected for an open model, to be honest. The pricing is where it gets really good. The API costs 0.834x per million input tokens and 2,001 per million output tokens, and cash hits are just 0.042 per million tokens. That makes it the cheapest flagship openweight model right now. It's cheaper than QN 3.8 Max and Kimmy K3. Although DeepSseek V4 flash is still cheaper if you just want the absolute cheapest option. You can get it through Tencent Cloud's token hub or through Open Router. So you can plug it into Klein Open Code or whatever coding agent you use. Now one thing to keep in mind, this is not a model you're going to run locally. The BF16 weights are around 1.8 TB and even the quantized FPA build needs about 900 gigs of memory. So you're looking at 16b200's minimum. So for most of us, the API or the apps are the way to go. And that brings me to the easiest way to use it, which is WorkBuddy. So WorkBuddy is 10 cents AI agent app for office work. It's a desktop app and it's kind of like a clawed co-work or manas type of thing. You give it a task and it breaks it down into subtasks, spins up multiple agents that run in parallel, uses the browser, reads your local files, runs code, and then delivers actual finished files. So reports, slide decks, spreadsheets, web apps, all that stuff. It has skills that you can enable for things like research, coding, and analytics. And it can connect to stuff like GitHub, notion, Google Drive, Gmail, and Slack as well. The best part is that Hi4 preview is free inside WorkBuddy for 2 weeks from launch. So you can go and test it right now without paying anything, which I know many of you would like. To set it up, just go to workbuddy.ai, I which will be linked below and download the international version for your Mac or Windows machine. Install it, register and log in. Then in the model selector at the bottom of the chat box, just select high for preview. That's it. If you want to compare it against other models, you can just switch the model in that same drop down and keep everything else the same, which is what I'll do for a couple of the tests. Now, let's get into the demos. I wanted to test the stuff that the model is supposedly good at. So, coding, 3D stuff, planning, long horizon execution, and multissource document works. So, I picked four tasks. The first one is a coding task, and it's a pretty hard one. I'm going to ask it to build a recreation of classic Super Mario style platformer gameplay using only the native HTML 5 canvas API and vanilla JavaScript. No phaser, no game engine. It has to use request Amig's brain for the game loop. Have full collision detection for terrain, bricks, and item blocks with mushrooms and coins. stomping enemies plus gravity, inertia, run acceleration, and proper jump physics. And I'm also asking it to draw the pixel art characters and tiles directly with the canvas API instead of using images. So I have work buddy open here with high for preview selected. Let me paste the prompt and send it. Now watch this. The first thing it does is create a plan. It breaks the whole thing into stages. The game loop, the physics, the tile map, the collision system, the entities, and then the rendering. Then it just starts writing the files. It's writing quite a lot of code here. You can see it's doing the physics constants, then the tile map, then the player class. Let's wait a bit. And it's now done. It actually opened the file in the browser on its own to check that it runs, which is pretty cool. Let me play it. Okay, so the movement feels pretty good. There's acceleration when you run. There's inertia when you stop. And the jump height changes depending on how long you hold the key. Let me hit this item block. And a mushroom pops out and slides along the ground. Let me jump on this enemy. and it squashes. The collision works on the bricks from below and from above as well. Everything is drawn with the canvas API, so there are no image assets at all. This is pretty amazing to be honest. This is a oneshot output, and I have seen much bigger closed models mess up the collision on this exact task. The second demo was a 3D one because the model is supposed to be good at 3D rendering. So, I'm asking it to create a 3JS nighttime neon street racing game with a thirdp person chase camera, wet reflective streets, neon signs, motion blur, nitrous effects, arrow keys to drive, drifting builds, nitrous, a wide-angle speed boost with blue, purple exhaust flames, AI opponents, live race standings, and a three-lap timer allin-one prompt. Let's send it and see. So, it plans it out again. It's setting up the scene, the lighting, the road, the buildings with emissive neon materials, the car physics, the AI opponents, and then the HUD. This one takes a little longer because there's a lot going on. Okay, it's done. Let me open it. And this looks really good. The reflections on the wet road are there, the neon signs are glowing, and the chase camera follows the car properly. Let me try drifting. You can see the nitrous bar filling up. And if I hit the boost, the camera field of view widens and there are the blue purple flames. The AI cars are actually racing and the standings on the top right update as I overtake them. The lap timer works, too. So, this is great for sure. The lighting and the environment design are the parts that impressed me the most. A lot of models get the physics right, but make this scene look flat and boring. This one doesn't. For comparison, I ran the exact same prompt with a different model in WorkBuddy, and it got the basic driving, but skipped the AI opponents entirely, and the nitrous didn't do anything. So, Hi-4 is clearly handling the multiconstraint stuff better. Here, the third demo is a productivity one, and this is where I think the model really shines. This is a long horizon multisource task. I have a folder with 24 reimbursement claims, plus policy documents with multiple versions, employee records, budgets, allowance usage, invoice history, and a bunch of emails. I'm asking it to act as an expense audit specialist. Check every claim against all the supporting materials. Classify each one as approved in full, approved with deductions or returned for more documentation, and then give me a batch summary with evidence-based findings for each claim. Flag any compliance or fraud concerns, calculate the total deductions, and list missing documents. This is the kind of task that would take a human, a full day or more. Let me send it. So, it starts by reading all the files in the folder. It figures out that there are two versions of the policy and it checks the dates on each claim to decide which version applies to which claim, which is exactly what you'd want. Then you can see it's going through the claims one by one, cross-checking the invoices against the emails and the budget file. This is going to take a while, so let me fast forward. Okay, it's done. And it delivered a word document with the summary and a spreadsheet with the claim by claim findings. Let me open the spreadsheet. So, every claim has a classification. The amount claimed, the deduction, the policy clause that was applied, and the evidence it used. It flagged three claims as potential duplicates because the same invoice number showed up twice with different dates, and it flagged one claim where the employees allowance had already been used up according to the usage file. It also caught two claims that were submitted under the old policy version after the new one had come into effect. The total deduction number at the bottom is correct as well. I checked it manually. I mean, it works well. It didn't hallucinate any evidence and it stayed consistent across all 24 claims, which is the hard part for long horizon stuff. Chef's kiss. Really good stuff. The last demo is a quick one. I asked it to do a deep research on the current state of openweight coding models and then turned that into a 10 slide presentation with proper design and a comparison table. It used the browser skill to go through a bunch of sources, pulled the numbers into a table, and then generated the deck. The slides actually look decent, which is not something I can say for most AI generated decks. and the numbers in the table matched the sources when I spot checked them. So that's great. So overall, what do I think? Personally, I think Hi4 preview is one of the best openweight models right now for agentic work. The coding is really solid. The 3D and gamedev stuff is arguably the best I've seen from an open model, and the long horizon document work is where it really beats the other open models in my testing. It's not perfect. It's still a bit behind Opus 5 and GPT 5.6 on the hardest stuff, and it's not something you can run at home, but the pricing on the API is really good, and the fact that it's Apache 2.0 means providers can host it cheaply, which is what matters for most people. If you want to try it, the easiest way is WorkBuddy where it's free for the next 2 weeks. The link is in the description, and if you want to use it in your own coding agent, it's on Open Router and Tencent Cloud's Tokenhub as well. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, [music] consider donating through the super thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, [music] give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye. >> [music]

Visit Retriever: https://rtrvr.ai/

In this video, I'll be telling you about RTRVR, also known as Retriever AI, and its new Free Mode, which lets you use its browser extension and cloud agent for free with sponsored ads. We’ll also explore browser automation, web scraping, job applications, reusable skill files, MCP server connections, and the features that still require a paid subscription.

--
Key Takeaways:

🚀 Retriever AI’s Free Mode lets you run eligible browser and cloud tasks without spending credits.
🌐 The AI agent can navigate websites, complete forms, scrape data, and organize information for you.
💼 Retriever can search for suitable jobs, compare roles, and help prepare applications for review.
📚 Students can use it to work through homework questions, understand solutions, and create practice exercises.
🧠 Personal skill files allow Retriever to remember your preferences, corrections, and recurring workflows.
🤝 Shared website skills help the agent learn how to navigate specifi
items.author: AICodeKing
items.transcript: [music] >> Hi. Welcome to another video. So, Retriever AI has launched free mode. You can now use its browser extension and cloud agent for free with a sponsored ad alongside your task. And this is an agent that can do the browser work for you. You can ask it to scrape websites, prepare job applications, or help with homework. It can open pages, work through forms, and collect the information you need. But, the feature I find more interesting is that it can learn how you work and save those lessons into skill files. So, when you come back with a similar task, it has something useful to remember. Today, let's look at how this works, what you can use it for, and which features still need a subscription. So, let's get right into it. Retriever takes a task written in normal language and works through it in the browser. You tell it what you want done, which websites to use, and what the finished result should look like. For example, you might want a spreadsheet of products from several stores, or you might have a resume and want help finding suitable jobs and filling out the applications. These are tasks where a lot of the work is opening pages, checking details, and copying information between places. That's the work you're giving to the agent. To get started, install the official Chrome extension, sign in, and enable free mode. You can then give it a task from the page you're already on. The extension is useful when you're working with websites you're signed into. You can also use Retriever through its cloud dashboard. I'll put links to both options in the description. Now, free mode covers the AI and cloud browser time for eligible runs without spending credits. A small sponsored card appears alongside the result, and daily fair use limits apply. Extra services such as enrichment beyond the included allowance can still use credits. So, you can start using the agent without buying a subscription, but keep those limits in mind if you're planning a large scraping job. Let's start with a scraping example. Suppose I'm comparing microphones for recording videos. I've opened a few product pages, and I want the details in one place. I would give it a prompt like compare the microphones on these pages. Make a table with the model, listed price, connection type, and product link. Leave anything you can't find blank. That gives the agent a clear job and tells it how to handle missing information. Then we can send it and check the table against the original pages. I'd look at whether it picked the correct product variant and whether it mixed up a sale price with the normal price. Those details decide whether the table is useful. You can use the same approach for software pricing, company directories, or a list of tools you're researching. Change the pages and the columns you want and you have another task to try. Now, job applications are another practical use case. You could tell it, "Use this resume to find junior front-end roles that allow remote work from my location. Show me why each role fits, then help me fill out the application for the one I choose. Pause before submitting." Retriever supports searching for roles, comparing them against your criteria, and preparing application forms for review. For me, the useful part is getting through the repeated fields and checking the requirements. I'd still read the finished application, especially any written answers about my experience. And for students, you can use the agent with homework and practice exams, too. For example, ask it to read a question on the page, work through the solution, and explain the step you don't understand. You could follow that with, "Give me another question using the same concept and check my answer." That would be a useful way to study directly from the material you already have open. Now, let's come to the skill files. This is where your corrections can keep helping after a task is finished. Retriever keeps personal skills that capture your preferences and recurring workflows. The agent can write and update these files when it learns something useful for future tasks. Let's say I want every product comparison to include a source link and I want missing prices left blank. Once that preference is saved, it can guide the next comparison, too. These are markdown files that you can read and edit yourself. Open the skills library to see what it has saved. The agent saves a lesson when it learns something durable, so it doesn't need to rewrite your memory after every simple task. There is also a separate set of shared website skills, according to Retriever. Successful runs help improve these site skills, and the team updates them as websites change. The idea is that useful knowledge about navigating a website can help other users, too. For example, imagine a site has a filter tucked inside a menu that the agent initially misses. A site skill could preserve the correct workflow, so future runs have that information available. Your personal skills describe how you want to work. The shared skills capture knowledge about the website itself. I like that approach, because correcting the same workflow every time gets annoying very quickly. The goal is fewer repeated mistakes across users. Although the agent still has to apply the saved guidance correctly. Now, Retriever also supports connecting MCP servers. If you haven't used MCP, it's a way for an agent to access tools supplied by another service. That could give it a way to query a database or work with an internal system alongside its browser tasks. In the extension settings, open the tool section, add the server's URL, and authenticate if the server requires it. The server's tools then become available to Retriever. For example, with a suitable database tool connected, you could ask it to compare information from a website against records you already have. The exact actions depend on the tools that server provides. There is a second MCP feature that matters for pricing. You can expose the Retriever browser extension through MCP, so another AI agent can operate your browser through it. That remote browser access requires a subscription. Connecting tools for Retriever to use and letting another agent control the extension are two different capabilities. Background schedules and triggers also remain paid, so manually starting a supported task in free mode is free. Having a check a website every morning or automatically start when an event happens is part of the subscription. As I'm making this video, the starter plan is listed at $9.99 a month with a monthly credit allowance for paid usage. Start with a task you already do regularly. If the agent handles it well and you want it running on a schedule, you have a reason to consider paying. Personally, the combination that interests me is free browser tasks with reusable skills. If I can give an agent my preferred output format, correct a workflow, and have those instructions help the next time, that makes it easier to fit into my work. For this channel, I'd start with collecting details from product pages and comparing tool pricing. Those are tasks where I can check the output quickly and see whether the agent saves me effort. If you want to try it, I'll leave the extension, cloud dashboard, and announcement in the description. Start with one task and see how it handles your website. Overall, it's pretty cool. Anyway, let me know your thoughts in the comments. If you like this video, consider donating through the Super [music] Thanks option or becoming a member by clicking the join button. Also, give this video a thumbs up and subscribe to my channel. I'll see you in the next one. Until then, bye. >> [music]
